column1: The world's oldest company ran for over 1,400 years
column2: Kongō Gumi, a Japanese temple builder, was founded in 578 AD. It traded independently until 2006, when it was absorbed by a larger construction firm.
column3: Longevity comes from doing one thing well for a very long time.

column1: Coca-Cola was first sold as a medicine
column2: In 1886 pharmacist John Pemberton sold Coca-Cola in Atlanta as a tonic at soda fountains. It became a mass-market drink through marketing, not medicine.
column3: Products often find their real market by accident.

column1: Nokia started as a paper mill
column2: Nokia was founded in Finland in 1865 as a pulp mill. Over the next century it moved into rubber, cables and finally mobile phones.
column3: Companies can reinvent themselves many times.

column1: The first barcode scanned was on chewing gum
column2: On 26 June 1974, a pack of Wrigley's gum was the first product scanned by a UPC barcode at a supermarket in Ohio.
column3: Huge systems often start with a humble test.

column1: Post-it Notes came from a failed glue
column2: A 3M scientist created a weak, reusable adhesive in 1968 that nobody could find a use for. Years later a colleague used it to stop bookmarks falling out of his hymn book.
column3: A failure in one context can be a hit in another.

column1: Supermarkets put milk at the back for a reason
column2: Essentials like milk are often placed at the far end of the store so shoppers pass more products on the way. Each extra aisle is another chance to buy.
column3: Store layouts are designed, not accidental.

column1: The 80/20 rule started with peas
column2: Economist Vilfredo Pareto noticed that 20 percent of the pea pods in his garden produced most of the peas. He then found that about 20 percent of people owned 80 percent of land in Italy.
column3: Uneven distributions show up everywhere.

column1: Prices ending in 99 really work
column2: Studies find that prices like £4.99 often sell better than £5.00 because shoppers anchor on the first digit. This is called the left-digit effect.
column3: Small framing changes move big decisions.

column1: Lego nearly went bankrupt in 2003
column2: After expanding into too many products, Lego faced heavy losses. It recovered by refocusing on its core bricks and cutting complexity.
column3: Focus can rescue a company that sprawled.

column1: Amazon started as an online bookshop
column2: When it launched in 1995, Amazon sold only books. Books were easy to ship and had a huge catalogue no physical store could stock.
column3: Start narrow, then expand.

column1: Monopoly was originally a warning about landlords
column2: The game began as The Landlord's Game, patented by Lizzie Magie in 1904 to show how land ownership concentrated wealth. Later versions dropped the message.
column3: Ideas can be repackaged to mean the opposite.

column1: The first credit card was for restaurants
column2: Diners Club launched in 1950 as a card for paying at restaurants in New York. It was a charge card, paid off in full each month.
column3: Big financial products often start in one niche.

column1: Free shipping thresholds raise basket size
column2: Many shoppers add items just to reach a free delivery threshold. Retailers set the line slightly above the typical order.
column3: Thresholds nudge behaviour more than discounts.

column1: The decoy effect sells more large drinks
column2: When a medium option priced close to the large is added, more people choose the large. The middle option exists mainly to make the big one look good value.
column3: Options can be designed to steer a choice.

column1: Netflix once mailed DVDs
column2: Netflix began in 1997 as a DVD-by-post rental service. It started streaming in 2007 and kept mailing discs until 2023.
column3: The winning business model may grow inside the old one.

column1: The stock market's opening bell is a real bell
column2: The New York Stock Exchange rings a bell to open and close trading each weekday. Guests ring it as a publicity event.
column3: Rituals help markets feel orderly.

column1: Compound interest is called the eighth wonder
column2: Money growing at 7 percent a year doubles roughly every 10 years. Starting earlier matters more than starting bigger.
column3: Time is the most powerful input.

column1: Most new restaurants struggle in their first years
column2: Studies of restaurant openings find a large share close within the first few years. Thin margins and high fixed costs leave little room for error.
column3: Passion needs a business model behind it.

column1: Logos rarely use purple
column2: Purple is among the least common main colours in big-brand logos; blue and red dominate. Colour choices signal trust, energy or luxury.
column3: Colour is part of the message.

column1: Shipping containers changed world trade
column2: Standard steel containers, introduced in 1956, cut the cost and time of loading ships dramatically. Global trade grew as a result.
column3: A boring standard can transform an industry.

column1: The paperclip has a surprisingly rich history
column2: The familiar double-loop Gem paperclip appeared in Britain in the 1870s and was never patented in its classic form. Many tried to improve it, but the design endured.
column3: Good enough can be unbeatable.

column1: Bubble wrap was meant to be wallpaper
column2: Inventors in 1957 tried to sell textured plastic as wallpaper. It failed, then found its use protecting fragile goods in shipping.
column3: Keep looking for the job your product does best.

column1: Sunk costs trap good decision-makers
column2: People keep investing in failing projects because of money already spent. The rational choice looks only at future costs and benefits.
column3: Past spending should not decide future spending.

column1: A small loss feels bigger than an equal gain
column2: Research by Kahneman and Tversky found losses weigh roughly twice as heavily as gains of the same size. This is called loss aversion.
column3: Framing a choice as a loss changes behaviour.

column1: Ford's moving assembly line cut build time sharply
column2: In 1913 Ford's moving line cut the time to build a Model T chassis from about 12 hours to around 90 minutes. Prices fell and sales soared.
column3: Process innovation can matter more than product.

column1: IKEA's flat-pack idea started with a table leg
column2: In the 1950s, an IKEA employee removed the legs from a table to fit it in a car. Flat-packing cut shipping and storage costs.
column3: Constraints can spark the best ideas.

column1: Starbucks is named after a fictional character
column2: The name comes from Starbuck, the first mate in Herman Melville's Moby-Dick. The founders wanted something evocative of the sea.
column3: Brands borrow stories.

column1: The first online sale is often dated to 1994
column2: In August 1994, a CD by Sting was sold online through a site called NetMarket, using encryption to protect the card details.
column3: Every giant market had a first customer.

column1: Most of a company's value can be intangible
column2: For many large listed firms, brands, software and patents make up most of the market value, not buildings or machines.
column3: The valuable stuff is often invisible.

column1: Anchoring shapes negotiations
column2: The first number mentioned in a negotiation tends to pull the final result towards it. Researchers call this anchoring.
column3: Going first can be an advantage.

column1: Toyota's cars are built just in time
column2: Toyota pioneered making parts only as they are needed. It cut waste and storage but made the company sensitive to supply shocks.
column3: Efficiency and resilience pull in opposite directions.

column1: Kodak invented the digital camera
column2: A Kodak engineer built a digital camera prototype in 1975. The company feared hurting its film business and was slow to embrace it.
column3: Protecting the old can block the new.

column1: The first Apple logo showed Isaac Newton
column2: Apple's 1976 logo was a detailed drawing of Newton sitting under an apple tree. It was soon replaced by the simpler apple.
column3: Simple usually wins in branding.

column1: Gillette's razor model sells blades
column2: Selling a cheap handle and profiting on replacement blades is known as the razor and blades model. Printers and coffee pods use it too.
column3: The profit is often in the refill.

column1: Many banknotes contain cotton, not paper
column2: US dollar notes are about 75 percent cotton and 25 percent linen. That makes them durable enough to survive the wash.
column3: Money is built to last.

column1: The price of a Big Mac tracks currencies
column2: The Economist's Big Mac Index compares burger prices to judge if currencies are over- or under-valued. It started as a light-hearted guide in 1986.
column3: Simple comparisons make complex ideas clear.

column1: Rolex is owned by a charitable foundation
column2: The Hans Wilsdorf Foundation owns Rolex. The founder set it up in 1945, and it holds the company today.
column3: Ownership structures can be unexpected.

column1: McDonald's sells mostly through franchises
column2: Most McDonald's restaurants are run by franchisees. The company earns rent and fees from them.
column3: Some businesses are property companies at heart.

column1: Coffee is one of the most traded commodities
column2: Coffee is grown in over 50 countries and traded worldwide. Millions of farmers depend on it for income.
column3: Your morning cup links to a global market.

column1: Free trials often turn into subscriptions
column2: Many people forget to cancel free trials. Firms count on this, which is why many countries now require clear reminders.
column3: Defaults drive behaviour.

column1: The term "boycott" comes from a land agent
column2: In 1880 Irish tenants refused to deal with Captain Charles Boycott. His name became the word for refusing to trade with someone.
column3: Collective action can make history.

column1: Fax machines predate the telephone
column2: Alexander Bain patented an early fax system in 1843, decades before the telephone was patented in 1876.
column3: Old ideas can wait for the right moment.

column1: Supermarkets pipe in the smell of bread
column2: Some stores use bakeries near the entrance so the smell of fresh bread greets shoppers. Pleasant smells can lift spending.
column3: Every sense can be used to sell.

column1: The number of business days in a year is about 252
column2: Stock markets are closed on weekends and holidays. That leaves about 252 trading days a year in the US.
column3: Finance runs on its own calendar.

column1: Bitcoin's creator is unknown
column2: Bitcoin was launched in 2009 by someone using the name Satoshi Nakamoto. Their true identity has never been confirmed.
column3: Some of the biggest ideas are anonymous.

column1: Branded goods often come from the same factory
column2: Many supermarket own-brand products are made by the same manufacturers as big brands, sometimes on the same lines.
column3: The label can matter more than the product.

column1: Loyalty schemes date back centuries
column2: In the 1700s some American merchants gave customers copper tokens to redeem for later purchases. Stamps and points followed.
column3: Rewarding repeat business is timeless.

column1: Companies can be older than countries
column2: Some businesses, like Japan's Nishiyama Onsen Keiunkan inn founded in 705, are older than many modern nations.
column3: Businesses can outlive governments.

column1: The Dutch East India Company issued the first public shares
column2: Founded in 1602, it sold shares to the public and is often called the first publicly traded company.
column3: Modern finance has old roots.

column1: Inflation means prices rise over time
column2: If inflation is 2 percent a year, prices double in roughly 35 years. Savings that earn nothing slowly lose value.
column3: Standing still can mean falling behind.

column1: Scarcity makes things seem more valuable
column2: Studies found people rated cookies from a nearly empty jar as tastier than identical ones from a full jar.
column3: Limited supply sells.

column1: Many famous brands started in garages
column2: Garages are a classic start-up story because they are cheap and available. HP's original garage in Palo Alto is now a historic landmark.
column3: Start where you are with what you have.

column1: Barcodes were inspired by Morse code
column2: Inventor Norman Joseph Woodland reportedly drew Morse code dots and dashes in sand and stretched them into lines.
column3: Ideas borrow from other fields.

column1: Price matching can reduce competition
column2: When shops promise to match rivals' prices, competitors have less reason to cut prices. Economists debate the effect.
column3: A promise to customers can also signal to rivals.

column1: Social proof drives sales
column2: People are more likely to buy something if they see others doing it. Reviews, ratings and "bestseller" labels exploit this.
column3: We follow the crowd more than we think.

column1: Most start-ups fail
column2: Studies of start-ups suggest the majority do not survive a decade. Running out of money is a common reason.
column3: Survival is the first win.

column1: Shipping costs used to dwarf product costs
column2: Before containers, loading and unloading could be a huge share of the cost of trade. Containers cut that dramatically.
column3: Logistics can decide what is worth making.

column1: Interest rates move house prices
column2: When borrowing is cheap, buyers can afford bigger mortgages, which tends to push prices up. Higher rates can cool the market.
column3: Money's price affects every other price.

column1: Coca-Cola's formula is a famous secret
column2: The company keeps its recipe in a vault in Atlanta. The secrecy itself has become part of the marketing.
column3: Mystery can be a brand asset.

column1: The 'paradox of choice' can stall buyers
column2: In a famous study, shoppers offered 6 jams bought more than those offered 24. Too many options can make people walk away.
column3: Less choice can mean more sales.

column1: The world's largest employer is not a company
column2: Organisations like the US Department of Defense and China's People's Liberation Army employ millions. Walmart is among the largest private ones.
column3: Scale takes many forms.

column1: A recession is often defined as two quarters of decline
column2: A common rule of thumb calls two consecutive quarters of falling GDP a recession. Official bodies use broader measures.
column3: Simple rules help, but definitions vary.

column1: Dynamic pricing changes by the minute
column2: Airlines and ride apps adjust prices based on demand, time and other factors. The same seat can cost very different amounts.
column3: Price is a moving target.

column1: Brand logos are often simplified over time
column2: Many companies have flattened and simplified their logos to work on small screens and app icons.
column3: Design adapts to the medium.

column1: Wrigley first sold soap and baking powder
column2: William Wrigley Jr. gave away chewing gum as a bonus with his products. The gum became more popular, so he switched.
column3: Listen to what customers want.

column1: The 'Veblen good' gets more desirable as it gets pricier
column2: Some luxury goods sell better at higher prices because the price signals status. Economist Thorstein Veblen described this.
column3: Price can be part of the product.

column1: The first company to hit a $1 trillion valuation was Apple
column2: Apple reached a $1 trillion market value in August 2018. Others followed soon after.
column3: Big numbers become normal quickly.

column1: Most money is digital
column2: Physical cash makes up only a small share of the money supply in many economies. The rest exists as bank balances.
column3: Money is mostly information.

column1: Credit scores date to the 1950s
column2: The FICO company was founded in 1956. Its credit scoring became widespread in US lending later.
column3: Algorithms decided lending long before AI.

column1: Patents last about 20 years
column2: In most countries, a patent gives an inventor exclusive rights for around 20 years. After that, anyone can use the invention.
column3: Protection is temporary by design.

column1: Long queues can attract more customers
column2: A busy restaurant signals quality. Some places are said to keep queues outside even with free tables inside.
column3: Popularity can be self-fulfilling.

column1: Moore's law guided chipmakers for decades
column2: In 1965 Gordon Moore predicted the number of transistors on a chip would keep doubling. The industry used it as a target.
column3: A prediction can become a plan.

column1: Warranties are often profitable add-ons
column2: Extended warranties sold at checkout can have high margins because many are never claimed.
column3: The extras can make the money.

column1: Thinking in opportunity cost helps decisions
column2: The cost of a choice includes the best alternative you give up. Spending an hour on one task means not spending it on another.
column3: Every yes is a no to something else.

column1: Lego bricks from 1958 still fit today
column2: Lego has kept the same basic stud-and-tube design since 1958, so old bricks connect with new ones.
column3: Compatibility builds loyalty.

column1: The first commercial was a 10-second clock ad
column2: In 1941 a Bulova watch ad aired on New York TV before a baseball game. It reportedly cost just a few dollars.
column3: Every giant ad industry started with a small slot.

column1: Gift cards often go unspent
column2: A share of gift card value is never redeemed. Retailers count some of that as profit, which is why they promote cards heavily.
column3: Unused value is still value to someone.

column1: Hotels use a "rack rate"
column2: The rack rate is a hotel's full published price. Few guests pay it, but it anchors discounts to look generous.
column3: A high reference price makes deals feel better.

column1: Most cars are white, black, grey or silver
column2: White, black, grey and silver dominate car sales worldwide because they are thought to hold resale value.
column3: Safe choices often win in big purchases.

column1: Tipping customs vary widely
column2: Tipping is expected in the US, modest in the UK, and can be seen as rude in Japan.
column3: Business rules are cultural.

column1: Nintendo started by making playing cards
column2: Founded in Kyoto in 1889, Nintendo produced hanafuda cards. It moved into toys and then video games much later.
column3: A company's first product rarely defines it.

column1: Samsung once sold dried fish
column2: Founded in 1938, Samsung began as a trading company dealing in groceries such as dried fish and noodles.
column3: Diversification can reshape a business entirely.

column1: Unilever's Lifebuoy soap launched in 1894
column2: Lever Brothers sold Lifebuoy as a hygiene soap in Victorian Britain. It is still sold in many countries today.
column3: Brands can outlast their founders by a century.
